paragraphs: Clifden is a small town in Co Galway. In summer, many tourists visit. In autumn, the town becomes very quiet.
The tourist office is closed until June. Some seafood restaurants are closed too.
A family gift shop opened a Christmas shop in October. Local people help the shop stay open in winter.
A big hotel stays open most of the year. It does not make money in winter. But it wants to keep its 75 workers all year.
A restaurant owner says it would make sense to close all winter. But he stays open because he cares about his staff. He closes in January so workers can go home.

Clifden, a tourist town about 80km west of Galway city, becomes very quiet after the summer visitors leave. The tourist information centre is closed until June 2027, and several seafood restaurants have shut for the season.

Lisa King, who runs a family gift shop, says the town goes quiet quickly after the arts festival in September. Local customers keep the shop going, and the family opened a Christmas shop at the back in October to bring in more sales.

The Abbeyglen Castle Hotel, which employs about 75 people, stays open most of the year. Its owner says winter does not make a profit, but keeping staff all year protects the hotel's culture. Many of its summer guests are Americans.

Declan Mannion, whose seafood restaurant opened in 1930, says it would probably make economic sense to close for the whole winter. He stays open out of loyalty to his staff, but closes in January so foreign workers can visit home.
The town is now trying harder to attract visitors outside the summer, for example with Christmas events.

Clifden, a tourist town about 80km west of Galway city, falls quiet once the summer crowds have gone. Its tourist information centre is closed until June 2027, and several seafood restaurants have shut for the season.

Lisa King, who runs a family gift shop, says the town empties rapidly after its September arts festival. Local custom keeps the business afloat, and the family opened a Christmas shop in October to boost sales during the off-season.

The Abbeyglen Castle Hotel, which employs around 75 staff, remains open for most of the year and targets customers from Galway and Dublin with golf packages. Its owner admits winter is not profitable but says retaining staff all year preserves the hotel's culture.

Declan Mannion, whose restaurant dates back to 1930, says closing for the entire winter would probably make economic sense, as quiet November nights hurt his margins. However, loyalty to his staff keeps him open until January, when he closes so international workers can go home.
Local councillors say the town is working harder to draw off-season visitors, including through a festive programme over three winter weekends.

Clifden, a Connemara tourist hub some 80km west of Galway city, lapses into a lull once the summer throngs depart. Its tourist office is shuttered until June 2027, and a number of seafood restaurants have closed for the season.

Lisa King, who runs a family gift shop, says the town empties with startling speed after its September arts festival. Loyal local custom keeps the business afloat, and the family has opened a Christmas shop to shore up takings in the lean months.

The Abbeyglen Castle Hotel, with a workforce of roughly 75, trades for most of the year, courting Galway and Dublin clientele with golf packages. Its owner concedes the off-season is unprofitable but argues that retaining staff year-round safeguards the hotel's ethos.

Declan Mannion, whose restaurant traces its roots to 1930, acknowledges that shutting for the whole winter would probably be the shrewder financial choice, since sparse November evenings erode his margins. Yet a sense of obligation to his staff keeps the doors open until January.
Councillors maintain that Clifden is redoubling its efforts to lure off-season visitors, not least through a festive programme spanning three winter weekends.
